newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: RTRS-PNG police get "shoot to kill" orders.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-PNG police get "shoot to kill" orders.

text.p: Police in the Papua New Guinea capital Port Moresby have been given "shoot to kill" orders to halt a surge of violence by armed gangs, the city's police commander said on Thursday.
"My policemen are under orders now to shoot to kill if confronted by armed criminals," commander Philip Taku told Reuters.
The prime minister of the South Pacific nation, Sir Julius Chan, has backed the orders.
"There has been an increase in armed hold-ups all targeting policemen. It's time we protect the innocent from the crooks," Chan told Reuters.
"It is time we turned the tide on the criminals."
Port Moresby police were told on Wednesday that they should shoot if they encounter armed gangs, known as "rascals".
Taku said the order followed a spate of violent attacks by the gangs and shoot-outs with police, said Taku.
Port Moresby is known as one of the world's most dangerous cities. Rising unemployment and urban drift has led to the growth of criminal gangs in recent years.
Large parts of the city centre are no-go areas for tourists and foreign residents, who live in houses surrounded by high walls and rasor wire.

On Tuesday night two policemen were held up in the city and their police vehicle used by criminals as a getaway car. On the same night, criminals opened fire on a police vehicle on the outskirts of the city.
Last week the wife of a senior police officer was shot dead in her car at a petrol station after refusing to surrender her car to the gang.
Speaking at a conference on security in Port Moresby, Chan said law and order, political stability and economic development were now the focus of Papua New Guinea's national security.
"Of all the menaces to our stability the most troubling is urban jobless growth, exacerbated by unplanned and excessive urban drift," Chan said.
"Internal disorder and unrest, extreme social dissatisfaction, can be a potent invitation for malicious forces to step in and disrupt the orderly conduct of our normal affairs," Chan said.
"We can do damage to ourselves quite easily, simply by allowing the demoralisation of our society...through social discontent caused by disaffected sections of our people.
"In a country such as ours, where aspirations and expectations can be unreasonably high, it provides a dangerous element in a potent cocktail for social disaster."
